analysis.one_liner: Cuts copyright terms to 28 years and retroactively shortens copyrights held by giant entertainment companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote; it drew zero cosponsors and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would shorten copyright protection for new works from life of the author plus 70 years to 28 years, renewable once for another 28 years. It would also reach back and shorten existing copyrights held by any entertainment or media company with a market value above $150 billion — a size only one company, Disney, meets. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, creators who build on older movies, shows, and other works would get free access to them much sooner, because works would enter the public domain after at most 56 years instead of nearly a century for corporate-owned works. Consumers and smaller studios would gain cheaper access to classic characters and stories. Authors of new works would lose out, though: their exclusive rights would end far earlier, cutting potential lifetime royalties and what their heirs could inherit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Creators reusing older works and consumers

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a copyright term of 28 years from the date a work's protection begins, renewable once for a second 28-year term if the holder applies during the final year — instead of the current life-of-the-author-plus-70-years rule for works created after 1977.

It applies retroactively to shorten copyrights owned by a person or company with a market capitalization above $150 billion that is classified in the motion picture or arts and entertainment industries, immediately cutting decades off those protections.

For licensees who were already operating under a license to such a copyright as of May 1, 2022, the bill lets them keep their rights for the shorter of half the remaining license term or 10 years, so some existing licensees are cushioned from the change.

analysis.who_pays: Large media and entertainment companies — effectively Disney, the only company that matches the bill's size-and-industry test — would lose decades of exclusive rights to their film and entertainment catalogs. Authors of new works and their families would also bear a cost, since their exclusive rights would end after at most 56 years instead of extending beyond their lifetime.
analysis.who_pays_short: Disney and creators of new works

drawbacks.text: The shortened 28-plus-28-year term applies to all new works, so individual authors lose decades of royalties they would otherwise keep for life and pass to their families — a cost to the very creators copyright is supposed to protect.

The retroactive provision is drawn so narrowly — over $150 billion market value, in motion picture or arts and entertainment industries — that it effectively singles out one company, raising serious constitutional questions about taking property and unequal treatment that would invite years of litigation.
The renewal requirement means a holder who misses the one-year filing window loses their rights entirely, adding a procedural trap for small creators who are not equipped to track filings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea of a shorter copyright term has real public benefit: works reach the public domain sooner and reuse of creative material is cheaper. But this bill does not implement that idea evenhandedly. It protects licensees but not owners, shortens protection for individual authors dramatically, and uses a market-cap threshold that appears designed to strike at one company rather than to reform copyright generally. Even supporters of shorter terms would likely have preferred a bill that did not target a single firm retroactively.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill on May 10, 2022.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and no further action — hearing, markup, or vote — was ever recorded.
No senator joined as a cosponsor at any point.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died without ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large entertainment companies kept their existing long-term copyrights untouched, and authors of new works kept the longer life-plus-70 terms. Anyone hoping for earlier public access to classic works got nothing, but the bill's narrowly targeted approach also never took effect, so no retroactive restructuring of one company's catalog occurred.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big media companies and copyright holders

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 10, 2022 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator from either party signed on, so the bill drew no measurable support from either side.

industries.industry: Major entertainment and media conglomerates (effectively Disney)
industries.note: The bill's retroactive clause — companies worth over $150 billion in motion picture or arts and entertainment industries — matches essentially one company and would cut decades off its exclusive rights to its film and character catalog. Its interest in preserving those long-term rights runs against the public's interest in earlier public-domain access, which is why the bill aimed at it.

industries.industry: Individual authors and creators of new works
industries.note: The 28-plus-28-year term applies to all new works, so writers, musicians, and filmmakers would lose decades of exclusive royalties they would otherwise hold for life and could pass to heirs. Small holders also face a renewal filing they could miss.

industries.industry: Smaller studios, publishers, and creators who reuse older works
industries.note: Works would enter the public domain far sooner, letting small studios, fan creators, and educators freely reuse classic movies, shows, and characters without licensing fees.
